common_name: Little Lamb Hydrangea (Fine-Textured Panicle Hydrangea with Small Dainty Blooms)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade; Little Lamb blooms on new wood, so it can be pruned hard in late winter without sacrificing that season's flowers.

directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, moderately fertile soil in full sun to partial shade; afternoon shade helps sustain flower quality through the hottest part of summer in zone 9. Little Lamb is a panicle hydrangea selected for smaller, more refined flower panicles made up of many tiny individual florets, giving the plant an airier, more delicate texture than the large, heavy blooms of cultivars like Limelight, and earning its name from the fluffy, lamb's-wool appearance of the massed small white flowers. Blooms open pure white in mid- to late summer and age to soft pink as temperatures cool in fall, held on sturdy stems that resist the flopping some large-flowered panicle hydrangeas suffer after rain. As with all Hydrangea paniculata, it blooms reliably on new wood, so hard pruning in late winter to shape the plant and encourage vigorous new growth does not sacrifice the coming season's bloom.

common_name: Quick Fire Hydrangea (Earliest-Blooming Panicle Hydrangea with Fast Color Change)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade; Quick Fire blooms several weeks earlier than most panicle hydrangeas and its flower color develops and deepens faster too, extending the season of colorful bloom.

directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, moderately fertile soil in full sun to partial shade, giving this larger-growing selection plenty of room to reach full size. Quick Fire was notable as the first panicle hydrangea bred specifically to bloom several weeks ahead of standard types, opening white flower panicles in early summer that begin shifting to deep pink and finally wine-red within weeks rather than the months typical panicle hydrangeas take, giving a longer overall season of colorful interest from a single shrub. Its sturdy, reddish stems hold the maturing flower panicles upright well, and the extended color change from white through pink to red-purple keeps the shrub visually interesting from early summer into fall. Like other panicle hydrangeas it blooms on new wood, so it tolerates hard pruning in late winter to control size or rejuvenate an older shrub without losing the coming season's flowers.

common_name: Rose Glow Barberry (Mottled Pink-and-Purple Foliage Dwarf Barberry)

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring or fall in well-drained soil in full sun to light shade; check state and local regulations before planting, as Japanese barberry is classified as invasive or restricted in a number of states due to its tendency to naturalize in woodlands.

directions: Plant in well-drained soil in full sun to light shade, since the mottled pink-purple color develops most intensely with good light exposure. Rose Glow is a compact, thorny barberry cultivar valued for new growth that emerges deep purple heavily mottled and splashed with rose-pink and white, giving each shrub a distinctive marbled, variegated look that matures to a more uniform reddish-purple as leaves age through the season. Its dense, twiggy, thorned branching makes it useful as a barrier planting or accent, and small yellow spring flowers are followed by red berries that persist into winter. Established plants are extremely drought-tolerant and low-maintenance, needing only an occasional shaping prune, but because Japanese barberry seeds into wild areas and displaces native understory plants in much of the eastern and midwestern US, gardeners should confirm it is not restricted or invasive in their area before planting.
sources: USDA NRCS Invasive Species Fact Sheet — Japanese Barberry

common_name: Neon Flash Spirea (Compact Spirea with Vivid Magenta-Pink Flower Clusters)

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring or fall in well-drained soil in full sun; a hard shearing right after the main early-summer bloom flush often triggers a second, lighter round of flowers later in the season.

directions: Plant in well-drained soil in full sun, where flower color and density are strongest; light shade is tolerated but reduces bloom. Neon Flash is a compact, rounded Japanese spirea selected for unusually vivid, saturated magenta-pink flower clusters that stand out more strongly than the softer pink of older spirea cultivars, blooming heavily in late spring to early summer over blue-green foliage. Shearing the shrub back by about a third immediately after the main bloom flush tidies its shape and often prompts a second, smaller flush of flowers later in the season. Established plants are tough, drought-tolerant, and low-maintenance, tolerating poor soil and urban conditions well, and the compact size suits foundation plantings, low hedges, and mixed borders where a large, sprawling shrub would be unwelcome.

common_name: Crimson Pygmy Barberry (Dwarf Mounding Deep Red-Foliage Barberry)

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring or fall in well-drained soil in full sun; check state and local regulations before planting, as Japanese barberry is classified as invasive or restricted in a number of states due to its tendency to naturalize in woodlands.

directions: Plant in well-drained soil in full sun, where the deep burgundy-red foliage color develops most intensely; shaded plants tend to green out and lose color saturation. Crimson Pygmy is one of the longest-established and most widely planted dwarf barberry cultivars, forming a tight, low, rounded mound of small reddish-purple leaves that holds its color from spring through fall, with small yellow spring flowers and red fall berries adding secondary interest. Its dense, thorny, compact habit makes it useful as a low hedge, foundation accent, or color contrast in mixed borders without the size of full-scale barberry cultivars. Established plants are extremely drought-tolerant, low-maintenance, and rarely need pruning beyond an occasional shaping cut, but gardeners should confirm local invasive-species regulations before planting, since Japanese barberry naturalizes readily and displaces native understory plants in much of the eastern and midwestern US.
sources: USDA NRCS Invasive Species Fact Sheet — Japanese Barberry
